summary: Redwood AE+SE ran an Optimize + Console walkthrough focused on prefix/KV cache strategies, batching configs and a cost model tailored to Kestrel's short chat sessions. Customer is interested in a pilot: 1) run benchmark using two model variants; 2) verify ~2.5x token-cost reduction with prefetch + sessionization; 3) confirm latency SLOs under 120ms p95. Key asks: SOC2 docs, sample cost workbook, and shared traces for tuning.
transcript:
Header: 2026-01-21 16:00 UTC; Duration 56m; Recorded on Redwood Console
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Rae (Redwood Product), Alex (CTO - Kestrel), Priya (Lead ML), Sam (Platform), Lena (Product)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we got about an hour, we'll run through the Optimize console playbook for batching and caching and then go into the cost sim. feel free to stop me.
[00:11] Alex: yeah thanks, Maya. quick background, we're building an in-app AI chat for support triage, short sessions, usually 40-120 tokens, lots of small requests. main goals are keep p95 under 120ms, and cut monthly token cost as much as possible.
[00:28] Priya: and we have strict data residency plus SOC2 on the road map, also would prefer dedicated pools if needed for SLA.
[00:37] Daniel: cool, that's helpful. i'm gonna share the console; we'll start with traffic shape then the prefetch/prefix caching options, show how the optimizer makes recommendations, then run a quick cost sim with your numbers.
[00:52] [screen share starts; faint keyboard noise]
[01:05] Daniel: alright, so, quick note—prefetch here means looking ahead in the session to populate the KV store with earlier tokens to avoid recompute on next prompt, whereas sessionization means keeping a short-lived KV cache keyed by session id. sometimes the transcript tool munges KV as 'k-v cache' or 'cahce' so apologies if the labels are a bit off.
[01:32] Priya: can you show the tradeoff matrix for latency vs token savings? that's our core question.
[01:40] Daniel: sure, on the left is throughput/latency impact—smaller batches lower latency but higher per-token compute, bigger batches amortize kernel overhead but raise p95. the console's optimizer recommends a batch size distribution based on your median sequence length and concurrency targets.
[02:02] [02:02] Daniel: so for Kestrel's profile (40-120 tokens, median 65, peak qps ~120) our recommendation is: session-affine routing + prefix prefetch horizon of 16 tokens, target batch size 8-16, concurrency cap per-GPU 48. that combo generally shows the best unit cost without blowing p95.
[02:22] Alex: how realistic is that 48 concurrency per GPU? in our infra we have bursty midday spikes.
[02:29] Daniel: it's conservative; it assumes gpus with 80 token context and depends on model variant. we'll bind concurrency in the router and use burst capacity for sudden spikes. the optimizer also suggests a fallback model that's cheaper but slightly higher latency for degraded capacity.
[02:46] Maya: quick interjection—on pricing, a lot of customers see 1.8–3x token cost reduction with prefix prefetch + session cache compared to naive per-request inference for short sessions. the exact number depends on hit-rate.
[02:59] Priya: what's the expected cache hit rate for prefetch horizon 16? we have pretty predictable prompts but sometimes follow-ons are open ended.
[03:07] Daniel: with deterministic UI flows you often see 40–65% prefix hit rates for horizon 8–16, but with chaty user inputs it drops. the optimizer can ingest your historical traces and estimate hit rate per endpoint.
[03:22] [03:22] Lena: what about cold starts and kiosk-like users that only have single-turn queries?
[03:26] Daniel: single-turns are the worst-case for prefetch; session cache won't help if there is no follow-up. for that mix we recommend hybrid: enable prefetch on flows with >1 predicted turns and keep batching tuned for small batch sizes, plus an L2 short-term TTL to catch immediate reasks.
[03:45] Priya: can the console auto-toggle prefetch per route? we have 12 micro-flows.
[03:51] Daniel: yes, you can set route-level policies—prefetch on, prefetch off, or adaptive. adaptive uses a lightweight predictor (recent session history) to decide; we'll demo the UI for that.
[04:05] [04:05] Daniel: switching to Optimize -> Recommendations tab. here you upload a trace or connect to a sample S3. the optimizer shows recommended batch-distribution, expected p95 uplift or latency cost, and an estimated monthly token spend delta.
[04:20] [04:20] Daniel: i'm loading a synthetic trace that approximates your profile... ok loaded. see the top chart — expected token reduction 2.3x with prefetch horizon 16 and session cache TTL 12 minutes, estimated p95 shift +18ms.
[04:38] Alex: 2.3x is great if it's real. what's the model assumption?
[04:43] Daniel: this sim uses a 7B open model we host (quantized) as the baseline; the console tags the model; we also tested a 13B floored quant variant—cost goes up ~1.7x but hit-rate benefits are similar. we can run both in the pilot.
[04:58] Priya: do you have numbers for compute vs inference cost—like how much of the savings come from skipping KV recompute vs better batching?
[05:06] Daniel: yes, in this trace roughly 60% of savings are from avoided KV recompute via prefetch/session, and 40% from better batching amortization. that ratio shifts with session length—longer sessions favor batching gains.
[05:21] [05:21] Sam: are there any gotchas for our infra? we use VPC private deployment for PII routing, and we're sensitive to KMS latency for key unwraps.
[05:31] Daniel: good call—KMS can add tail latency to decryption flows, so for Private deployments we recommend caching unwrap results short-term in the host and using client-side key encryption where possible. Redwood Private supports an HSM integration so you can keep keys local. we'll include the SOC2/KMS note in the security doc.
[05:52] Maya: going to walk through the cost-simulator sheet next, it's where we convert hit-rate and batch metrics into monthly $ spend. i'll share my screen.
[06:02] [06:02] [screen switches to spreadsheet]
[06:07] Maya: top inputs—requests per day, median tokens per request, expected follow-up rate, model unit cost per token, and number of GPUs reserved. below that the sim breaks down tokens avoided, GPU-hours, and service fee.
[06:21] Maya: using your numbers (120 qps peak, median 65 tokens), the default sim shows $X,XXX baseline. with prefetch horizon 16 + session TTL 12 min + batch distribution target 12 we drop to about 0.43x of baseline cost (so ~57% savings). i put a conservative hit rate 45% in here.
[06:41] Priya: can you export the raw assumptions? our finance folks will want the math.
[06:45] Maya: yes, i'll export the workbook and include scenario tabs (best/typical/worst).
[06:50] Alex: what's the expected effort for the pilot? we want minimal engineering lift.
[06:54] Daniel: typical pilot is 2–3 weeks engineering + a 48-hour benchmark run. steps: 1) share trace; 2) Redwood runs initial sim and recommends batch/prefetch config; 3) we deploy a test canary route with monitor hooks; 4) benchmark and tune. we can do most of the simulation and initial config on our side—your team only needs to add the small SDK call to tag sessions for sessionization.
[07:16] Priya: how invasive is the session tagging? we use a serverless front end with ephemeral lambda.
[07:21] Daniel: a simple header (session-id) is enough; no heavy state. the sessionization strategy stores KV per session key in the runtime's ephemeral store—nothing persistent unless you opt in. for serverless, we suggest sticky routing or an affinity token in the request.
[07:35] Lena: can you show the live console alerting for regressions? we want to avoid quality degradation from quantized model variants.
[07:42] Daniel: yep, Optimize hooks into the eval suite—you can attach prompt sets and the console will surface quality regressions by comparison ( rouge-like metrics or custom evals ). it also ties regressions to rollouts so you can auto-fallback to safety model.
[07:58] [07:58] Daniel: quick demo — here's a canary request stream; you see latency histogram, token savings, and a quality score card. if quality drops beyond threshold we flag and optionally revert.
[08:12] Alex: we've had issues with opaque fallbacks in other vendors—how explicit is the routing policy?
[08:18] Daniel: routing policies are explicit JSON policies you can edit in the console. they include priority tiers, region, and model flavor. rollback is immediate and logged.
[08:28] Priya: back to the cost model, would prefetch increase memory pressure on GPUs because of longer KV states?
[08:34] Daniel: yes, prefetch increases KV footprint per active session—optimizer estimates memory delta and will recommend quantization or smaller batch sizes if memory becomes a bottleneck. plus we can shift some cache to CPU if needed but that impacts latency.
[08:50] Maya: small note—the optimizer suggests a quantization profile that preserves most QA quality but reduces activation memory by ~30%. we call it 'q4-compat'.
[08:59] Sam: about auditing—do we get event logs for cache hits/misses and who called what? for compliance.
[09:06] Daniel: yes, audit logs include route, session id (hashed), cache hit/miss, batch id, and model variant. logs are exportable to your SIEM. we'll include sample log schema in the security pack.
[09:18] [09:18] Alex: any competitors we should be worried about—low level?
[09:22] Maya: customers often compare with Bedrock for hosted ease, but the main difference is our unified runtime + explicit cost tooling. Anthropic is also mentioned sometimes re: model quality.
[09:34] [09:34] Priya: can we run a dry-run where Redwood simulates our traffic but doesn't touch our prod keys? we can anonymize traces.
[09:41] Daniel: absolutely. we only need a redacted trace with tokens hashed or lengths and turn structure preserved; no PII. once we run the sim we share the exact config recommended.
[09:52] Rae: i'm going to show the 'what-if' slider in the cost-sim — you can drag hit-rate, adjust batch sizes, and see projected monthly spend change in real time.
[10:00] [10:00] Rae: sliding hit-rate from 30% to 60% updates token-saved and cost-saved instantly; it's helpful for stakeholder discussions.
[10:12] Alex: nice. can the console output be exported as a short pdf executive summary for procurement?
[10:16] Maya: yes, exportable 'summary pack' includes assumptions, charts, recommended config, and risk notes.
[10:22] [10:22] Priya: a couple specifics—1) we have GDPR users in eu-west, can you pin routing by residency? 2) can the KV store be encrypted in transit with customer-managed keys?
[10:32] Daniel: yes to both. residency routing is a first-class policy and KMS integrations support CMKs; for Private deployments you can use HSM. we'll attach the security architecture doc.
[10:45] Alex: any scalability limits on session TTL? if we set 12 minutes and our user abandons and comes back after 20 minutes, will they lose the cached context?
[10:53] Daniel: TTL is configurable—12 minutes was a guideline. longer TTL means more memory but higher chance of reuse. the console will show evictions over time so you can tune TTL vs mem pressure.
[11:05] [11:05] Priya: what about monitoring model drift—if we reduce tokens with prefetch might we mask quality regressions?
[11:12] Daniel: good point. Optimize ties cost metrics and quality signals; we surface both so you can see if savings correlate with quality dips. the eval hooks let you run golden prompt sets periodically.
[11:25] Maya: ok last part: logistics for pilot—i'll email the workbook and export, Daniel will scope the benchmark and Sam we'll need your S3 link for traces.
[11:35] Alex: that works. rough timeline—pilot kickoff next week, benchmark week after.
[11:40] Maya: perfect, we'll follow up with a calendar invite and the shared folder. thanks everyone.
[11:45] Priya: thanks, that was helpful.
[11:48] [11:48] meeting ends

Notes on transcription: some domain words transcribed as 'kv cahce' or 'k v cache', model names abbreviated; speaker labels were manually corrected in places, so timestamps may shift a few seconds.
